summary_grc: ὁ Λύσανδρος τὰς ναῦς τῶν Ἀθηναίων πρὸς τῇ γῇ λαμβάνει· ἡ δὲ Πάραλος εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἀπαγγελοῦσα ἀποπλεῖ.
summary_en: 405 BC: for four days the Athenian fleet rows out to challenge Lysander, and each afternoon the crews scatter ashore. On the fifth day a flashing shield gives the signal, and the Spartans take almost the whole fleet on the beach. Xenophon, Hellenica 2.1.27–29, with cuts: orders in indirect speech, ἐπάν + subjunctive, αἱ μέν … αἱ δέ.
caption_grc: Λύσανδρος δʼ εὐθὺς ἐσήμηνε τὴν ταχίστην πλεῖν.

original.note: Xenophon, Hellenica 2.1.28–29, with cuts only (the two opening sentences are ours; a clause about the market and the captured sails is left out). The battle was in late summer 405 BC. Xenophon, then in his twenties, was probably in Athens; he wrote the Hellenica decades later, in exile, beginning where Thucydides breaks off.

grammar.md:
**Reading Xenophon: orders, signals and a divided fleet.** From this lesson on the story is Xenophon's own text, shortened but not rewritten. Everything outside the core list and the track list is glossed.

**1. Orders in indirect speech.** Verbs of telling, ordering and signalling take an **infinitive** for the action ordered (the person is dative with λέγω, accusative with κελεύω):

| verb | example | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| εἶπε + dat. + inf. | εἶπε τοῖς ἑπομένοις … ἆραι ἀσπίδα | told those following to raise a shield |
| σημαίνω + inf. | ἐσήμηνε τὴν ταχίστην πλεῖν | gave the signal to sail |
| σημαίνω + inf. | ἐσήμηνεν εἰς τὰς ναῦς βοηθεῖν | signalled (the men) to run to the ships |
| κελεύω + acc. + inf. | ἐκέλευσε τοὺς ἑπομένους ἆραι | ordered them to raise |

**2. ἐπάν + subjunctive** 'as soon as, whenever' (ἐπάν = ἐπειδάν = ἐπειδὴ ἄν, 8.2): ἐπὰν κατίδωσιν 'as soon as they see'.

**3. Dividing a group: ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ.** αἱ μὲν … αἱ δὲ … αἱ δέ 'some … others … others'; οἱ δὲ καὶ ἔφυγον 'and some even fled'.

**4. Participles doing the work.** ἰδών (aorist: when he saw), φεύγων (present: while fleeing), διεσκεδασμένων τῶν ἀνθρώπων (genitive absolute, perfect: since the men were scattered), ἀπαγγελοῦσα (future: to report). The perfect participles ἐκβεβηκότας, ἐσκεδασμένους, διεφθαρμένα describe a state: 'landed', 'scattered', 'ruined'.

**5. Crasis and elision in the text.** δʼ = δέ, παρʼ = παρά, καθʼ = κατά before a rough breathing (ἑκάστην).

culture.title: Xenophon and the end of the fleet
culture.md:
**Xenophon** (about 430 to after 355 BC) was an Athenian of good family and a follower of Socrates. In 401 he joined the Greek mercenaries of Cyrus (hist.7), later served with the Spartans, and was exiled from Athens; he lived for years on an estate near Olympia. His **Hellenica** ('Greek affairs') starts in 411 exactly where Thucydides stops and runs to 362. It is plainer than Thucydides: short clauses, direct speech, vivid detail, and a soldier's eye for how things were done.

By 405 Athens depended on one last fleet in the **Hellespont**, the narrow strait through which the grain ships from the Black Sea came. The Athenians camped on an open beach at **Aegospotami**, far from a market, so that the crews had to scatter to buy food; the exiled Alcibiades rode down from his castle to warn them and was sent away (2.1.25–26). The Spartan commander **Lysander** (formally only second-in-command, since Spartan law forbade anyone to be ναύαρχος twice, but in fact in charge), paying his crews with Persian money, waited four days and struck on the fifth.

Of about 180 triremes only nine escaped: **Conon** with eight went to Cyprus, and the state trireme **Paralus**, the ship that carried the city's official messages, sailed for Athens with the news. Lysander put the Athenian prisoners to death, some 3,000 men according to Plutarch. The bronze ram found off Athlit in Israel (from a warship of about 200 BC, but the same weapon) shows what these ships fought with.
